newsitem.title: UK: Expectations for Club Med in EMU rise - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Expectations for Club Med in EMU rise - JP Morgan.

text.p: Market expectations of a broad-based launch for European economic and monetary union -- encompassing the so-called 'Club Med' countries -- increased last week, according to financial prices monitored by JP Morgan.
The probability assumed by the market that Spain, Italy and Portugal will join Germany and France in the first wave of EMU rose four to five percentage points, the U.S. house said.

The market now sees a 78 percent chance that Portugal will be in the single currency at the start, up from 73 percent a week ago. Spain has risen five points to 76 percent, while Italy's assumed probability increased to 60 percent from 56, JP Morgan's "EMU calculator" showed.

European Union finance ministers this week welcomed the convergence plans of Spain and Portugal, giving a powerful shot in the arm to those states' currencies and assets and boosting expectations a wide group will begin EMU on January 1, 1999.

Those expectations were bolstered by this week's official forecast of an 18 billion marks shortfall in Germany's 1997 tax revenues, which stoked speculation the EMU entry criteria would have to be relaxed -- opening the door wider for the 'Club Med'.
The perceived probability of Sweden joining in 1999 increased to 60 percent from 54, while Ireland was up three points at 63.
Finland and Britain bucked the trend, however, slipping to 76 and 49 percent from last week's 77 and 53 respectively.

Britain's reading of 53 percent last Friday marked a leap in EMU expectations after the Labour Party -- widely viewed as more euro-friendly than their Conservative predecessors -- took power here for the first time since 1979.
The U.S. investment firm's calculator --which is derived from the interest rate swaps market -- showed the readings for France and Belgium remained at 100 percent.
JP Morgan points out there is a reasonable margin of error in overall probability levels of between three and five points.
The probabilities are derived from the actual swap spread, an in-house assumption of what the spread would be if EMU were not a factor, and the expected spread after EMU participation, which is zero.
